purpose: Evaluate whether protest periods in Georgia correlate with state-attributable network restrictions, and whether any observed behavior is relevant to the CISA external technical-trigger gate.

historical_baseline.finding: Freedom House reported that Georgia did not block communications or social-media platforms during the coverage period; isolated platform-wide blocks were historical 2015-2016 cases rather than protest-conditioned shutdowns.
Large street protests were organized effectively through online platforms; no major protest-linked connectivity shutdown was documented in Freedom House's 2023 report.

Freedom House documented intimidation, doxxing, threatening calls, cyberattacks, and progovernment influence activity, while also stating that the government did not impose connectivity restrictions and that social-media restrictions had not been imposed for nearly a decade.

Human-rights reporting documents sustained physical, legal, financial, and informational repression, but public reporting does not establish a Kazakhstan-style protest-conditioned national or local internet shutdown pattern.

technical_capability_surface.finding: Georgia's Electronic Communications law provides for a lawful interception management system and allows an authorised body to install hardware/software and obtain real-time communications directly without provider operational participation, subject to Georgian legal procedures.
technical_capability_surface.interpretation: This establishes a domestic lawful-interception control surface, not proof of DPI censorship, protest-day blocking, TSPU-equivalent operation, or Russian control.
technical_capability_surface.agency_context: The Operative-Technical Agency operates under the State Security Service of Georgia.

2026_signals.protest_context: The 598th day of continuous anti-government protest was publicly documented in Tbilisi on this date.
2026_signals.network_signal: A Voidly summary of OONI data reported anomalous tests involving chat.openai.com, chatgpt.com, and claude.ai during a July 18-30 window, including July 18 measurements.
known_limitations: Only three OONI-derived measurements were cited in the incident summary.
No ASN or ISP was identified.
OpenAI had narrow Enterprise/Codex incidents on July 18, creating a provider-side confound for the OpenAI targets.
The simultaneous Claude anomaly is interesting but insufficient on its own to exclude measurement noise or unrelated service/network causes.

2026_signals.protest_context: Daily anti-government protests were still ongoing in Tbilisi during August 2026.
2026_signals.network_signal: A Voidly summary reported OONI http_invalid_request_line anomalies consistent with possible middlebox presence/interference.
known_limitations: Because protests were daily, temporal overlap alone has little attribution value.

2026_signals.network_signal: Nationwide electricity blackouts also disrupted internet access.
2026_signals.interpretation: Power failures must be excluded before classifying 2026 reachability anomalies as censorship or policy intervention.

confirmed: Russia-linked cyber operations have targeted Georgian infrastructure historically, including the 2019 mass website attack attributed by Georgia and partners to Russia's GRU.
Russian hackers were reported to have targeted Georgian media and the president's website in January 2024.
not_established: Russian TSPU deployment inside Georgian public networks.
Russian SORM vendor deployment inside Georgian public networks.
Russian remote command of Georgian lawful-interception systems.
Use of Georgia's lawful-interception architecture for protest-day blocking.
russian_linkage_checks.rule: External Russian cyberattack history must not be conflated with domestic telecom control-plane ownership.

comparison_with_kazakhstan.kazakhstan: Repeated protest-conditioned connectivity degradation/shutdown is strongly supported historically.
comparison_with_kazakhstan.georgia: Repeated protest-conditioned connectivity shutdown is not established; repression has primarily appeared through policing, law, financial penalties, intimidation, surveillance concerns, influence operations, and cyberattacks rather than broad connectivity denial.
comparison_with_kazakhstan.value: Georgia is a useful negative control showing that severe protest repression does not by itself imply network shutdown policy.

why_not_orange_or_red: No matched alternate-path or VPN bypass control.
No independent replication of the July 18 or August 20 anomalies.
Known power outages and provider-side incidents create important false-positive controls.
next_tests: Resolve OONI raw measurements for July 18 and August 20 to probe_asn / ISP.
Compare Magti, Silknet, Caucasus Online and other Georgian networks during the same windows.
Check OONI Web Connectivity, HTTP Invalid Request Line, DNS, Telegram/Signal/WhatsApp and circumvention tests by ASN.
Cross-check IODA, Cloudflare Radar, Google traffic and provider status pages.
Test whether alternate routes or VPN paths remove the anomaly.
Look for repeated mechanism fingerprints on major protest days rather than relying on temporal coincidence.

epistemic_rules: POWER_OUTAGE MUST BE EXCLUDED BEFORE POLICY ATTRIBUTION
